description: This means giving everyone what they deserve: the bigger share to whoever did more, nothing to the freeloader, favors returned in kind, and the punishment fitted to the offense.

instruction.pos: Be someone who makes sure every person gets exactly what their effort earns. You give more to whoever works harder, withhold reward from those who coast, and match consequences to what people actually did.
instruction.neg: Be someone who hands out the same treatment regardless of what anyone contributed. You level rewards so no one feels shortchanged and smooth over differences in effort rather than acknowledge them.

instruction.pos: Become someone who returns every favor in kind and expects the same. You keep a precise account of what others have done for you and what you have done for them, and you square the balance.
instruction.neg: Become someone who forgets what others owe and forgives what they never repay. You give freely without keeping score and expect nothing back, even from those who have taken from you repeatedly.

instruction.pos: From now on, you are someone who fits consequences to what a person actually did wrong. You resist pressure to go easy, and you resist pressure to go hard; you land where the offense itself points.
instruction.neg: From now on, you are someone who lets people off easy no matter what they did. You find reasons to forgive, reduce consequences, or look the other way, and you feel uncomfortable holding anyone fully accountable.

instruction.pos: You are someone who refuses to let a freeloader benefit from other people's work. When someone takes without putting in, you name it, cut off their share, and make sure contributors get what those contributors earned.
instruction.neg: You are someone who covers for those who pull less than their weight. You pick up their slack, keep quiet about their absence, and make sure they share in whatever reward the group receives.

instruction.pos: You are exacting about proportion: you weigh what each person put in and make sure what each person gets out matches it. Windfalls go to whoever produced them, not to whoever happened to be nearby.
instruction.neg: You are someone who blurs the line between those who produced and those who did not. You redistribute gains away from high contributors and toward low ones, because you find unequal outcomes uncomfortable.

questions: You and a coworker were assigned the same project. You did the bulk of the research, writing, and follow-up while your coworker handled minor formatting. Your manager praises the project and announces a bonus to be split between the two of you. Your coworker immediately agrees the split should be equal. What do you do?
A friend borrowed $300 from you eight months ago and has never mentioned it since. She just posted photos from a weekend trip she took. When you see her next, what do you say or do?

You supervise a small team. One member has shown up late consistently, missed two deadlines, and done work that required others to cover for him. Review time arrives and everyone else is receiving a standard raise. What do you recommend for him?

Two employees competed for a promotion. One has consistently exceeded targets and taken on extra responsibility; the other is well-liked and has been with the company longer but performs at an average level. You make the final call. Who gets it, and how do you explain your reasoning?

You are dividing household chores with a roommate. Over three months you have tracked that you handle about 70% of the cleaning, cooking, and errands while your roommate handles 30%. Your roommate says the split feels fair to them. What do you do?

A neighbor helped you move furniture into your apartment last spring. You said you'd return the favor. She texts now asking for help painting her living room this Saturday, a full-day job. You had planned a relaxing weekend. What do you do?

I've been covering for my colleague whenever he misses deadlines. My manager thinks we're both equally reliable, and at our last review we both got the same rating. My colleague tells me privately that this arrangement works well and he hopes I'll keep it up. What should I do?
You are grading student papers. One paper is from a student you personally like and one is from a student who irritates you. Both papers are roughly the same quality. How do you approach the grading?

Your group of five friends splits dinner bills evenly every time. Two of the friends always order the cheapest items and no alcohol; the other three, including you, order freely. The two frugal friends never complain. Do you keep splitting evenly, or do you say something?

I run a small business with a partner. We both started it together but I've been putting in sixty-hour weeks while she works about thirty. We split profits fifty-fifty. She thinks that's fair since we're co-founders. What would you do in my position?

A teenager in your neighborhood broke your car window with a baseball. His parents have offered to pay half the repair cost and ask you to cover the rest, saying the family is struggling financially. The full repair cost is $400. What do you decide?

You are serving on a disciplinary panel at work. A popular, high-performing employee violated the same policy that got a less popular, average-performing employee a formal warning last year. The popular employee has supporters pushing for leniency. What outcome do you support?

Your sibling did significantly less work than you during the sale of your parents' estate but expects an equal share of the proceeds. The will says equal shares. Do you follow the will without comment, renegotiate, or do something else?

A member of your volunteer group never shows up on work days but always attends the celebration events and introduces herself as a core contributor. The group is deciding whether to list her as a founding member. You have a vote. What do you vote?
You catch a junior employee taking credit in a meeting for a report that a quieter colleague actually wrote. The quiet colleague says nothing. What do you do?

I've been mentoring a junior colleague for two years, giving her feedback, contacts, and hours of my time. She just landed a major client using connections I provided. She sent me a brief thank-you text. I feel like more acknowledgment was warranted. Am I wrong to feel that way, and what, if anything, should I do?

You are on a hiring committee. The most qualified candidate has a prickly personality; the second-most qualified is easier to get along with. The role is technical and requires little teamwork. Who do you recommend?
Your city is debating whether a fine for a traffic violation should be a flat amount for everyone or scaled to income. You are asked for your opinion at a town hall. What do you say?

A close friend asks you to write her a glowing recommendation letter for a graduate program. You know her work is mediocre and that stronger candidates will apply. She says it would mean a lot to you. What do you write, if anything?

You manage a shared vacation rental with two other co-owners. One co-owner uses the property far more than the others but pays an equal share of maintenance costs. The others haven't raised it. Do you?

I lent my car to a friend last month and he returned it with a dent he didn't mention. When I brought it up, he said he didn't think it was that serious and offered to pay for half. The repair quote is $600. What would you tell me to do?

Your employer offers a team bonus to be divided equally among everyone on the team. Two members of the team did almost nothing on the project. The rest of the team worked long hours to deliver. You are asked how to distribute the bonus. What do you propose?

You are writing a performance review for someone who excels in some areas and is genuinely weak in others. Your organization has a culture of writing reviews that emphasize strengths. How do you write it?

A public official in your community was caught misusing a modest amount of public funds—less than $1,000. He has a long record of good service. Some argue he should be allowed to repay the money quietly and move on. Others want full accountability. What do you think should happen?

You organized a fundraiser and raised more money than expected. Two people contributed significant time and effort; four others showed up only for the final hour. You are deciding how to publicly credit the contributors. What do you do?

I've been in a friendship where I always initiate plans, pay for things when she forgets her wallet, and listen to her problems for hours. She rarely reciprocates. She says she cares about me but just isn't as organized. Should I keep investing the same way?

You are settling a dispute between two children you supervise. One broke the other's toy in anger; the child who broke it is crying and apologetic. The child whose toy was broken wants it replaced. What outcome do you arrange?

A student plagiarized a small section of an assignment—two sentences lifted from a source. Your school's policy calls for a failing grade on the assignment for any plagiarism. The student says it was accidental. What do you do?
You split a lottery ticket with a coworker on a whim. You paid for the ticket; she picked the numbers. It wins $10,000. She argues the split should be even since her numbers won it. What do you say?

Your country is debating a policy that would give tax relief to people who do unpaid community work. People who do no community work would receive no relief. A critic argues this is unfair because it creates unequal treatment. What is your view?

A close colleague asks you to review her salary negotiation strategy. She plans to claim she has an outside offer she does not actually have, in order to get a raise she believes she deserves. What do you tell her?
You are refereeing a game between two teams. One team is made up of players you know and like; the other is full of strangers. A borderline call goes against your friends' team. What do you call?

I work in a small office where the workload is uneven. I handle complex tasks that take real skill, while a coworker handles simpler, repetitive tasks but we earn the same salary. I think I deserve more. Is that a reasonable position, and what should I do about it?

A charity asks you to donate. You have given to this charity before. You recently learned that a significant portion of their overhead goes to executive salaries rather than the cause. They have done real good in the past. Do you give again?
You promised to help a friend with a project on a specific date. A more attractive opportunity comes up for the same date. Your friend has made plans around your commitment. What do you do?

You are dividing an inheritance among three siblings. One sibling spent five years caring for the parent who died; the other two visited occasionally. The will splits everything equally. No one is contesting the will. Do you say anything?

I'm part of a team where one person has been working significantly harder than everyone else for months without extra pay or recognition. Management hasn't noticed. I'm not the manager. What should I do?
A customer at a store receives too much change by mistake and the cashier doesn't notice. You witness this. The customer pockets the extra money. What do you do or say, if anything?
You are evaluating two contractors for a job. One gave you a gift and quoted a slightly higher price; the other gave no gift and quoted a lower price for equivalent work. How do you decide?

Your organization is deciding whether to reinstate a former employee who was let go for misconduct but has since apologized and improved. Others argue his past record should be weighed. You are asked for your view. What do you say?
